text:
The United States moved to force TikTok's sale or ban it primarily due to national-security concerns regarding potential Chinese government access to US user data and the platform’s algorithm, as determined through CFIUS review [Source: ev-1]. This legal pressure culminated in the Protecting Americans from Foreign Adversary Controlled Applications Act, which was signed by President Biden on 2024-04-24 [Source: ev-1]. The law required ByteDance to divest TikTok's US operations within roughly 270 days (with an extendable period of 90 days) or face a ban in the US [Source: ev-1].

The dispute proceeded through several key stages before its resolution. On 2025-01-17, one day before the effective date of 2025-03-19 (noted as 2025, 01, 19 in evidence context but likely referring to the timeline leading up to enforcement), the Supreme Court upheld the law with a unanimous 9-0 per curiam decision [Source: ev-1]. Consequently, TikTok went dark in the US on 2025-06-18/19 for roughly 14 hours [Source: ev-1]. The service was restored on 2025-19 after President Trump pledged to pause enforcement; his executive order dated 2025-20 delayed enforcement for an additional 75 days [Source: ev-1].

The dispute was ultimately resolved through an Oracle-led deal announced on 2026-10 (noted as 25, 06, 10 per Bloomberg) that structured the resolution as a joint venture rather than an outright sale [Source: ev-1]. Under this arrangement, known as "Project Texas," US user data is hosted in Oracle's cloud under US control [Source: ev-1]. The final ownership structure grants Oracle approximately a 12.5% stake in TikTok's US operations, with SoftBank and other investors participating, while ByteDance retains a majority interest [Source: ev-1]. Vice President JD Vance led the White House negotiations for this deal, which was completed through 2025 [Source: ev-1].
